A Romanesque basilica on a hill across the Arno, on one of the highest points of Florence. It honours Saint Minias, by legend a soldier in the Roman army martyred under the emperor Decius, who after his beheading carried his own head up the hill to his hermitage. There was a chapel on the spot by the 8th century. Bishop Alibrando began the present church in 1013, with gifts from the emperor Henry II. Its monastery was Benedictine, then Cluniac, and since 1373 has been run by Olivetan monks.

The front, begun probably about 1090 and finished in the 12th century or later, is faced in marble in geometric patterns and crowned by the eagle of the cloth merchants' guild, the Arte di Calimala, which looked after the church from 1288. Inside, the choir is raised above a large crypt, the oldest part of the church. The inlaid floor and the marble pulpit and screen date from 1207, and a mosaic of 1297 in the apse shows Christ between the Virgin and Saint Minias.

Later Florentines added Michelozzo's Chapel of the Crucifix (1448) and the chapel of the Cardinal of Portugal (1460 to 1468), a tomb chapel by Antonio Manetti and the Rossellino brothers with work by Luca della Robbia and the Pollaiuolo brothers. During the siege of Florence in 1530 the bell tower served as a gun post, and Michelangelo had it wrapped in mattresses against enemy fire. The walls he threw up were made into a fortress by Cosimo I de' Medici in 1553, and since 1854 they have enclosed a cemetery, the Porte Sante.
